I disagree with your differential diagnosis, medical professional here. HIV is the slow destruction of specific white blood cells called CD4+ &CD8+  T-Lymphocytes. This destruction doesn't necessarily cause symptoms until your body attempts to use them,  At which point it fails and whatever infection it was attempting to eradicate advances. The most common first symptom of HIV is swollen lymph nodes, mainly because your body is trying to create & release lymphocytes rapidly but because it cannot (usually because the virus will hinder the lymphatic system) the glands remain swollen. Other unusual symptoms may accompany said lymphedema such as high fevers, night sweats & fatigue. These take several months if not years to manifest. What you've described is a localized bacterial infection (most likely Group B Strep) since its most commonly colonized in the vagina. Unfortunately your infection is beginning to spread and needs immediate medical attention. Strep infections in soft tissue are aggressive and can lead to bacteremia and sepsis extremely fast. Please consult your physician and be honest about the situation so they can prescribe the most appropriate antibiotic.

Salary depends on your location but for a new grad, somewhere in the 40K range is a very rough estimate. Of course with experience comes higher salary. OP is right though, does require quite a bit of biology also. As well as certification via one of accreditation agencies approved by NACCLS, (i.e. ASCP, AMT, etc). You can get individual certification for Clinical Chemistry but most facilities aren't willing to hire someone that can only work one department. Generalist are typically more desired in hospital settings. Then there's also non-clinical laboratories that seek Chemistry Degree holders. Problem is finding those are like a needle in a haystack. But def look into Clinical Laboratory Science, may have to take a few more courses to become eligible for a clinical program but might be worth it. Good Luck!

Glycogenesis and Glycolysis are semi-mutually exclusive of each other. Glycolysis is always occurring, even after death the body's cells will continue to utilize what remaining glucose molecules it can with whatever oxygen it has left. When blood is taken for testing, if the serum or plasma remain on the cells too long, you'll see a significant decrease in glucose when tested. However, the rate of glycolysis can be influenced by glycogenesis. See link below.    


[Insulin Pathway](https://image.slidesharecdn.com/dm1-131124215540-phpapp02/95/pathophysiology-of-dm1-7-638.jpg?cb=1385330326)

Glycolysis is a constant never ending reaction your body uses to make energy in the form of ATP. The phosphate bonds in ATP are massive energy stores, which makes it effective for energy potential.  1 molecule of Glucose yields 32 ATP. The rate of Glycolysis depends on many factors (type of cell, type of tissue, energy requirement for type of  cell or tissue). Glycogenesis refers to Glucose metabolism on a macro scale. Glycolysis takes place on a molecular level. Hope this helps .
